Twenty-one comments

Floating Crowbar

I believe this tune to be a composition of BRENDAN McGLINCHEY,
the great Co. Armagh fiddler. He recorded it himself on a record he made on the Belfast “Outlet” recording label sometime in the 70s.

↳ Posted by Kenny on December 26th, 2001.

Floating Crowbar

This has also been recorded by the Battlefield Band who say that it was a popular session tune in Scotland in the 80s

↳ Posted by Noel Jackson on June 29th, 2002.

The Floating Crowbar

Arty McGlynn on the album “McGlynn’s Fancy” recorded the version of the tune I am trying to learn.
Before I start, I was wondering does anybody know the following, what guitar tuning he is using? Are there tabs available for this tune? Is it a hard one to master?
All help on this is appreciated, as I don’t have much time to learn it.

↳ Posted by tedtrad on May 19th, 2004.

Small error ?

I had a look at this for tedtrad. I think there’s a small, but significant typo(?) here - the “b” note in the 5th bar of the 2nd part should be a “B”. Otherwise, I think this is an accurate transcription. Difficult on guitar, I would think ( unless you’re Arty McGlynn, of course). Incidentally, “McGlynn’s Fancy” isn’t in the “Recordings” section yet. Maybe someone could remedy that?

Who composed The Floating Crowbar?
https://thesession.org/discussions/29053#comment617830

↳ Posted by Tawny on January 2nd, 2012.

From the other thread…

I spoke to Richie (brother of Finbar) Dwyer who said it’s one of Finbarr’s compositions. He (Richie) mentioned a Michael McMahon who was present when Finbar composed it.

According to Richie, Finbar has composed around thirty tunes. Some are pretty weird. Michael, another of Richie’s brothers, is another composer of “traditional” tunes.

Richie himself seems to sprout tunes.

Re: The Floating Crowbar

I’m wondering if there is any back story about the name of this tune… some weird or seemingly nonsensical names - especially for those of us foreigners who don’t have a lot of knowledge of the Irish culture of the old days - have a rational explanation or basis, just one we don’t have the background knowledge or dialect to understand. Or maybe it’s just a bit of 70’s silliness… Anybody know? Apologies if this has been covered before!

↳ Posted by Benjamin Ruth on February 21st, 2021.

Re: The Floating Crowbar

Finbarr Dwyer was asked why he so named the tune.
His reply reportedly was: “Well, if a pitchfork can ramble…”

↳ Posted by Jerry O'Donnell on February 21st, 2021.

Re: The Floating Crowbar

suitably enigmatic… thanks

↳ Posted by Benjamin Ruth on February 21st, 2021.

Re: The Floating Crowbar

Regarding the name. It’s my understanding, from a friend of mine who worked on building sites for most of his working life, that “the floating crowbar” refers to a crucial point in the process where concrete is starting to “go off”; when it’s in an intermediate state between liquid and solid and you know it’s at that critical point because it appears still to be quite liquid but a crowbar will float on it… I can’t vouch for the accuracy of that statement (or even that I’ve managed to convey the gist properly) but he’d have very little cause to make it up.

↳ Posted by Aidan Crossey on April 5th, 2022.

Re: The Floating Crowbar

Only 20 years late! But regarding Tetrad’s query, I think the great Artie played it in either standard guitar tuning or dropped D but for reasons best known to the man himself, he capoed the guitar at the 3rd fret thus effectively playing it in F.

↳ Posted by Martin Street on October 22nd, 2024.

Re: The Floating Crowbar

I learned this on guitar from the Artie McGlynn recording and I’ve played it in F with the capo at 3 and in D without the capo. Since it’s a solo album, I would say the capo is a really nice touch. It brightens up the sound of the guitar and really makes the whole thing shimmer.

Also, re tuning, I believe Artie McGlynn typically plays in Drop D.
